806.title: Bhaddiya's "what bliss"
806.hook: a former ruler, sitting under a tree, keeps sighing "ah, what bliss" (Udana 2.10)
806.howItsDone: Teachers in the Theravada tradition tell Bhaddiya's story to show the ease of a simple life in the forest, and the phrase aho sukham, ah, what bliss, is sometimes repeated in talks on letting go.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ananda's grief, when friend and teacher were gone. Your line was all directions dark. Today, a sigh of a very different kind.

Ah, what bliss. Ah, what bliss. A monk sits at the foot of a tree in the forest, saying it over and over. Other monks overhear, and they worry. This man, Bhaddiya, used to be a ruler. They figure he's remembering the palace, the comfort, the power, and missing it all. So they go and tell the Buddha. The story is in the Udana, a collection of short teachings that close with an inspired saying.
screen: `AH, WHAT BLISS.` → `THE MONKS WORRY.` → `THEY TELL THE BUDDHA.`

segments.voice: First, the question. The Buddha sends for Bhaddiya and asks him straight out: is it true you keep saying, ah, what bliss? It's true, he says. Second, the reason. When I was a ruler, Bhaddiya says, there were guards inside my private rooms and outside them, inside the town and outside it, around the whole country. And even guarded like that, I lived afraid, anxious, always watching. Now I go to the forest, to the foot of a tree, to an empty hut, alone, and I'm not afraid. I'm not anxious. I live at ease, he says, with a mind like a wild deer. Third, the wild deer. A deer in the forest owns nothing. It isn't defending a border or counting its guards. It's light on its feet and needs little. That's the bliss he means: not what he gained, but what he no longer has to protect. Fourth, the misunderstanding. The other monks heard the very same words and took them for a sigh for the past. He meant the opposite: he was glad the past was over. Then the Buddha speaks the inspired saying that closes the story, about someone with no anger inside, gone beyond being this or that, free of fear, happy, without sorrow, whom even the gods can't see. Ah, what bliss, from a man who had every guard he could want, and was afraid.

segments.voice: Rest your attention on something small that asks nothing of you: the warmth of a mug, light on a wall, the breath itself, arriving without being asked. Then notice what you don't have to guard right now, no message to answer, no problem to solve, at least for these minutes. If a quiet ah rises, let it; if it doesn't, that's fine too.
Sukha. Happiness, ease: the word behind the former ruler Bhaddiya's sigh under a tree, not longing for the palace, but glad to have nothing left to guard. Today's word.
Your line: ah, what bliss. Sometimes ease is simply having nothing left to guard. Day eight hundred six, done.

807.title: Rahula's verses
807.hook: the son who says he is doubly fortunate, son of the Buddha and heir to the teaching (Theragatha, Rahula)
807.howItsDone: The Vinaya traces its rule of parents' consent before a child is ordained to Rahula's story and his grandfather's grief, and communities that keep the Vinaya keep that rule with it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhaddiya sat under a tree and kept sighing, ah, what bliss: sukha. Your line was ah what bliss. Today, a son with two inheritances.

Give me my inheritance. A small boy says it, walking behind a monk. In the Vinaya's telling, the Buddha has come back to his father's city, and Rahula's mother sends their son after him to ask for what a father owes. The boy follows, telling the monk he likes the shade he casts. The Buddha doesn't hand him land or gold. He asks Sariputta to ordain the boy. Much later, Rahula sings about that inheritance himself, in the Theragatha.
screen: `GIVE ME MY INHERITANCE.` → `NOT LAND, NOT GOLD.` → `THE BOY SINGS LATER.`

segments.voice: First, the name. They call me Rahula the fortunate, he says, and I'm fortunate both ways: once because I'm the Buddha's son, once because I've come to see the teaching clearly. One inheritance by birth, one by practice, and he names both plainly. Second, what the second one asked of him. He describes himself as he was: blinded by pleasures, caught in a net, wrapped in craving, bound by carelessness, like a fish in the mouth of a trap. Being the Buddha's son, in his own telling, didn't spare him any of that. The first inheritance came free. The second he had to take up. Third, what he found. The pleasures are thrown off, he says, Mara's bond is cut, craving is pulled out root and all. He has grown cool, quenched. Fourth, back to the boy in the road. In the Vinaya, the Buddha reflects that the inheritance the boy asked for brings trouble with it, and chooses to give him another kind, the kind nobody receives by blood. And the text doesn't end on the gift. Rahula's grandfather, King Suddhodana, comes to the Buddha in pain. He has watched a son leave, and now a grandson. He asks that no child be ordained without the parents' consent, and the Buddha agrees and makes it a rule. So the second inheritance cost someone something, and the Vinaya keeps that grief on the page. Doubly fortunate, and the story behind the song shows both sides of the gift.

If you pray, give thanks for both in your own way; if not, simply hold them side by side, the given and the taken up.

Your line: doubly fortunate. One gift came by birth, and one he had to take up. Until tomorrow.

808.title: Sona's bleeding feet
808.hook: the soft-footed monk who walked until his feet bled, and learned about the lute (Theragatha, Sona Kolivisa)
808.howItsDone: The lute simile is retold in meditation teaching when a student is straining too hard or drifting too loose, and the Vinaya traces the monks' allowance of sandals to him.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rahula called himself fortunate twice, by birth and by the teaching. Your line was doubly fortunate. Today, a monk who tried too hard.

Blood on a walking path. In the Vinaya's telling, a young man named Sona Kolivisa was raised so softly that hair grew on the soles of his feet. Then he became a monk, and he walked up and down in meditation, back and forth, until his feet split open. The text says the path looked like a place where cattle are slaughtered. He was giving it everything, and it wasn't working.
screen: `SOFT FEET, HARD PATH.` → `BLOOD ON THE WALKING PATH.` → `EVERYTHING, AND NOTHING YET.`

segments.voice: First, the thought. Alone in the grove, Sona reasons with himself: I'm one of the disciples who strive hardest, and still my mind isn't free. My family has wealth. I could go home, enjoy it, and do good with it. It's an honest thought, and the text doesn't mock it. Second, the question. The Buddha knows his mind and comes to him, and he doesn't start with a teaching. He asks about Sona's old life. When you lived at home, were you skilled at the lute? Yes. When the strings were wound too tight, could it be played? No. Too slack? No. And tuned to an even pitch, neither too tight nor too slack? Then, yes. Third, the turn. Just so, the Buddha says: effort pushed too hard runs into restlessness, and effort too slack runs into laziness. So set your effort evenly, tune your faculties to each other, and take your aim from there. The answer came out of Sona's own hands. Fourth, the sandals. In the Vinaya, after Sona's mind is freed, the Buddha offers him sandals for those soft feet. Sona hesitates: people will say he gave up great wealth and now clings to footwear. He'll wear them only if every monk may. And the Buddha allows sandals for the whole order. One man's bleeding feet became a kindness for everyone after him. The Theragatha keeps a song under his name, and behind it stands that lute.
screen: `I COULD GO HOME AND DO GOOD.` · `WERE YOU SKILLED AT THE LUTE?` · `TUNED TO AN EVEN PITCH.` · `SANDALS FOR EVERYONE.` · then, large: `NOT TOO TIGHT.`

segments.voice: Take your shoes off if you can, let your feet rest flat on the floor, and let the breath come at its own pace, not pulled long, not held short. If you catch yourself trying hard to relax, that's a tight string, so let it slacken; if you drift off, that's a slack one, so come back to the soles of your feet. Somewhere between the two, there's an even note.
Vina. A lute: the instrument the Buddha used to teach Sona, who had walked until he bled, that effort is tuned, neither too tight nor too slack. Today's word.
Your line: not too tight. Effort, like a lute, gets tuned. That's day eight hundred eight.

809.title: Nanda's vanity
809.hook: the half-brother confesses he was vain and restless until he learned (Theragatha, Nanda)
809.howItsDone: In Theravada teaching, Nanda's story is told as an example of the Buddha meeting a student where he is, and his verses sit among the Theragatha's songs of the early monks.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sona walked until his feet bled, and the Buddha asked him about a lute, a vina. Your line was not too tight. Today, a monk whose song opens with his vanity.

In one sutta, Nanda comes to the Buddha in pressed robes, with ointment around his eyes and a glazed, shining bowl in his hands. He's the Buddha's half-brother, son of the aunt who raised them both. The Buddha looks at him and says, in effect: this isn't fitting for someone who left home out of faith. Go live in the forest, wear robes made of rags, and stop caring about the pleasures of the senses. Later, Nanda made his own song about who he'd been.
screen: `PRESSED ROBES, A SHINING BOWL.` → `THIS ISN'T FITTING.` → `HIS OWN SONG.`

segments.voice: First, the confession. Nanda's verses in the Theragatha are short, and they open without a defense. Through careless attention, he says, I was given to adornment. I was restless and fickle, burning with desire. No excuse about youth or family. Just: I was vain. Second, the way out. Through the skillful means of the Buddha, kinsman of the sun, he says, I practiced properly and pulled my mind out of the pull of becoming. Third, what skillful means meant in his case. The Udana tells the story. Nanda wants to leave the order. He can't stop thinking of a young Sakyan woman who, as he left home, asked him to come back soon. So the Buddha takes him, the story says, to a heaven, and shows him heavenly women more beautiful than anyone he's seen. Nanda admits the woman at home no longer compares. The Buddha promises him such company if he practices, and Nanda practices, for a reward. The other monks find out and call him a hired hand, working for wages. Ashamed, he goes off alone, practices in earnest, and is freed. Then he releases the Buddha from the promise. He no longer wants the prize. Fourth, what his song leaves out: no heaven, no prize, no teasing monks. Only the plain admission and the plain gratitude. The story is strange and vivid. The song is spare. A man who once dressed for an audience sings verses with nothing dressed up.

810.title: Vangisa the poet
810.hook: the poet-monk who praised the Buddha in verse on the spot (Theragatha, Vangisa)
810.howItsDone: Vangisa's poems are kept in the Theragatha and in a chapter of the Samyutta named for him, and verses of praise to the Buddha, the teaching and the community are chanted in Buddhist communities to this day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nanda opened his song by admitting his vanity. Your line was I was vain. Today, a monk whose gift was words.

It occurs to me, Blessed One. It occurs to me, Fortunate One. In a sutta of the Samyutta, a monk stands up in the middle of a teaching, puts his robe over one shoulder, raises his joined hands and says it, twice. Something is coming, and he can't sit on it. The Buddha answers: then let it come to you, Vangisa. And Vangisa speaks a poem of praise, right there, to the whole gathering.
screen: `IT OCCURS TO ME.` → `LET IT COME TO YOU.` → `A POEM, RIGHT THERE.`

segments.voice: First, who he was before. In his verses in the Theragatha, Vangisa looks back: once, drunk on poetry, I wandered from village to village, town to town. Then I saw the Buddha, gone beyond all things, and faith arose in me. He didn't stop being a poet when he became a monk. The poetry turned toward something. Second, the danger in the gift. Another sutta in the same collection says that Vangisa, because of his quickness with words, looked down on other monks, good and steady ones. Then he caught himself and turned his poetry on his own pride: drop the conceit, he tells himself, it leads nowhere good. The same tongue that praised could also sneer, and he knew it. Third, the question. After one of his poems of praise, the Buddha asks what a writing teacher might ask: Vangisa, were these verses thought out beforehand, or did they come to you on the spot? On the spot, he says. Then, says the Buddha, let a few more come. He doesn't warn him off spontaneity. He asks for more. Fourth, what the praise is for. Vangisa's poems praise the Buddha, Sariputta, the teaching, the gathered monks. Praise, in these suttas, isn't flattery or a performance for the poet. It's seeing clearly what's good in front of you and saying so, out loud, while the person can hear it. For a man who once used words to look down on people, that's a turn worth singing about.
screen: `DRUNK ON POETRY, VILLAGE TO VILLAGE.` · `THE GIFT THAT LOOKED DOWN.` · `PLANNED, OR ON THE SPOT?` · `SAYING WHAT'S GOOD, OUT LOUD.` · then, large: `PRAISE, IN VERSE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person whose goodness you've seen up close and maybe never named, and let a single line about them form; it doesn't need to rhyme or be clever, only true, like she stays when things get hard. Patibhati. It occurs to me: what Vangisa the poet said when a verse arrived, a monk who learned to use his gift to praise what's good, on the spot. Today's word.
Your line: praise, in verse. Praise that sees clearly is a gift, not flattery. Day eight hundred ten, done.

811.title: Old age, in their words
811.hook: monks and nuns alike write about ageing without flinching
811.howItsDone: In Theravada monasteries, reflections on aging, sickness and death are part of the chanting, and the scenes of the Buddha's own aging body are retold when teachers speak about impermanence.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vangisa the poet stood up mid-teaching and let a poem come: patibhati, it occurs to me. Your line was praise in verse. Today, the elders and the aging body.

An old man is sitting with his back to the evening sun, warming it. A younger man is rubbing his arms and legs. That's how a short sutta in the Samyutta opens, and the old man is the Buddha. The younger is Ananda, his attendant. And as he works, Ananda says what he sees, out loud, to his teacher's face.
screen: `A BACK WARMED IN THE EVENING SUN.` → `ANANDA SAYS WHAT HE SEES.` → `TO HIS TEACHER'S FACE.`

segments.voice: First, what Ananda says. It's a wonder, he tells the Buddha: your skin is no longer clear and bright, your limbs are slack and wrinkled, your body leans forward, and your senses have changed. He doesn't say you look great for your age. Second, how the Buddha answers. So it is, Ananda. Youth is subject to aging, health to sickness, life to death. He doesn't correct Ananda, and he doesn't comfort him. He agrees. Then he speaks verses that are startling from a calm teacher: shame on you, wretched old age, maker of ugliness. This lovely body, the verses say, is trampled down by age, and no one escapes death. Third, the cart. In the long sutta of his last journey, the Buddha says it himself: I'm old now, worn out, near the end. Like an old cart kept going by being tied together with straps, this body is kept going. It's at ease, he adds, only when he rests in a deep, quiet meditation. Fourth, the sisters said it too. Earlier in this block, Ambapali sang of her black hair gone white, her body changed, and her refrain that the truth-speaker's word holds true. Sona sang of finding strength late. Monks and nuns, the teacher and the taught, all look straight at the same thing. In these texts, seeing it plainly is part of the path, not a failure of it, and it's said kindly, to a teacher's face.
screen: `YOUR SKIN IS NO LONGER CLEAR.` · `SO IT IS, ANANDA.` · `AN OLD CART HELD WITH STRAPS.` · `THE SISTERS SAID IT TOO.` · then, large: `WITHOUT FLINCHING.`

segments.voice: Feel the body you're sitting in and notice one place that has changed, a knee, your eyes, your hands, the way you get up from a chair, and look at it the way Ananda looked: plainly, kindly. Let one true, simple sentence form, like my hands are slower than they were, and let it sit there without adding a complaint or a cure.
Old age. In the elders' words, it's named plainly: the slack skin, the bent back, the cart held with straps, said kindly and without pretending. Today's word.
Your line: without flinching. The body is named as it is, and named kindly. Until tomorrow.

812.title: Which voice is yours
812.hook: of all the elders' songs, one sounds like you
812.carry: each kept in its own temper
812.howItsDone: The Theragatha and Therigatha keep each poem under its singer's name, so a reader can come back to one voice at a time.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ananda told his teacher plainly how old he looked, and the Buddha said, so it is. Your line was without flinching. Today, the week ends with a listen back.

Ah, what bliss. I was vain. Fortunate both ways. It occurs to me. So it is. Five lines from one week, and no two of them sound alike. A former ruler sighing under a tree. A half-brother confessing. A son counting his blessings. A poet who couldn't sit on a poem. An old teacher agreeing that he's old. The elders' songs aren't one voice. They're a crowd. Before this block of songs closes, a quiet question: which voice is yours?
screen: `FIVE LINES, FIVE VOICES.` → `NOT ONE VOICE, A CROWD.` → `WHICH ONE IS YOURS?`

segments.voice: First, the voices that confess. Nanda: I was given to adornment. Uttama, among the sisters, left her cell again and again before the day she stayed. Talaputa, the actor, argues with his own restless mind: when will it be? These songs start with the trouble and don't hide it. Second, the voices that delight. Bhaddiya, once a ruler with guards inside and outside his palace, now sits at the root of a tree, unafraid: ah, what bliss. Mahakassapa loves his rocky hills. Subhuti tells the rain to go ahead and fall. Third, the voices that grieve and turn. Ananda after the passing, every direction dark. Kisa Gotami, praising good friends, then telling her grief, then the deathless. Patacara, drawing down a lamp's wick with a needle. Fourth, the plain voices. Mutta, glad to be free of the mortar, the pestle and her crooked husband. Ambapali, her hair once black. Rahula, counting what he inherited. Sona, taught by a lute, not too tight. No one in these collections is asked to sound like anyone else. Each song keeps its singer's name and its singer's temper. The tradition kept the delighted and the mourner, the poet and the penitent, side by side. So the question isn't which voice is best. It's which one you'd recognize if you heard it across a room.
screen: `VOICES THAT CONFESS.` · `VOICES THAT DELIGHT.` · `VOICES THAT GRIEVE AND TURN.` · `PLAIN VOICES.` · then, large: `WHICH VOICE IS YOURS.`

segments.voice: Let the singers pass by one at a time, the confessor, the one in the hills, the mourner, the plain speaker, and notice not the one you'd like to be but the one you already sound like on an ordinary day. Recall one line of that song as closely as you can, and let it repeat slowly in time with the breath; if two voices come, let them take turns.
Gatha. A verse: what the elders' songs are built from, a crowd of named voices confessing, delighting, grieving, speaking plainly, each kept in its own temper. Today's word.
Your line: each kept in its own temper. No singer had to sound like anyone else. That's day eight hundred twelve.
